error_modes.label: Recognition of when CRM enhances mission performance and flight safety

texts.0: SP, due to complacency on a profile flown repeatedly without incident, did not recognize any point at which CRM affected mission performance or flight safety. SP handled the sortie as a single-seat task and produced no coordination input at the briefing, in flight or at the debriefing. The IP had to stop the item and direct the required crew actions before the profile could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to complacency toward crew coordination in a familiar pattern, treated CRM as relevant only where flight safety was already threatened and not where it would have improved mission performance. SP acted only after the IP had stated the point verbally more than once, and the coordination that followed came after the phase of flight in which it was useful. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially task-focused approach to the profile, missed the first opportunity where crew coordination would have improved mission performance. SP recognized the omission without prompting, stated the coordination requirement and applied it for the rest of the sortie. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP recognized accurately and without delay when CRM enhanced mission performance and flight safety, and stated it in the briefing, in flight and in the debriefing. Coordination was applied at the point where it produced an effect rather than after the event. All CRM items applicable to the sortie were covered without IP prompting.
texts.4: SP identified crew coordination opportunities before they became necessary and used them consistently across briefing, flight and debriefing. SP linked each specific CRM behavior to the resulting gain in mission performance and flight safety. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on recognizing when CRM enhances mission performance and flight safety, but did so almost only in the safety-related cases and rarely in the mission-performance ones. The trend across the sortie was toward recognition after the IP raised the subject rather than before. SP is expected to state the CRM benefit on his/her own initiative on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Use of the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight applicable items

texts.0: SP, due to unfamiliarity with the publication, did not use the IFG/CRM matrix chart at any point and could not locate the items applicable to the sortie. No CRM item from the matrix was covered in the briefing and none was highlighted in the debriefing. The IP had to open the chart and work the applicable items with SP before the grade sheet could be completed.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete pre-brief preparation, opened the IFG/CRM matrix chart but highlighted items unrelated to the profile flown. SP selected the correct items only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and the discussion of them was pushed to the end of the debriefing. No further action beyond the extended debriefing was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed review of the chart during mission planning, first highlighted a general matrix item instead of the one matching the maneuver flown. SP recognized the mismatch without prompting, returned to the IFG/CRM matrix chart and selected the correct item in time for the discussion. No IP direction was required.
texts.3: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart accurately and without delay to highlight the CRM items applicable to the sortie. The items selected matched the profile flown and the areas covered in the debriefing, and were presented in the standard sequence.
texts.4: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight the applicable items and tied each one to a specific event of the sortie. The selection was complete, correct and needed no revision by the IP, with negligible deviation from the expected standard.
texts.marginal: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart and met the standard, but selected the minimum number of items and needed a second look at the chart to confirm two of them. The trend was toward picking the familiar items rather than those matching the profile actually flown. SP is expected to preselect the applicable matrix items during mission planning on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Application of the CRM concept when planning maneuvers

texts.0: SP, due to planning the profile as an individual rather than as a crew task, did not apply the CRM concept when planning the maneuvers and briefed no division of duties, no lookout responsibility and no knock-it-off criteria. Sequence and area limits were left undefined until the maneuvers were reached. The IP had to stop the briefing and rebuild the maneuver plan before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to time compression in the planning phase, applied the CRM concept to only one of the briefed maneuvers and left the rest without an agreed division of duties. SP added the missing content only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and the plan was completed after the briefing was formally over. No IP intervention in flight was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete first run through the profile, planned the opening maneuver without stating clearing and lookout responsibilities. SP recognized the omission before the briefing ended, restated the plan with the CRM elements included and flew it as restated. No IP prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP applied the CRM concept to the maximum extent when planning the maneuvers, with duties, clearing responsibility, entry parameters and knock-it-off criteria agreed before flight. The plan was stated accurately and without delay and the maneuvers were flown as planned.
texts.4: SP planned every maneuver as a crew task, including the contingencies and the point at which each maneuver would be discontinued. The plan was complete and unambiguous, required no addition by the IP, and deviations from the expected standard were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard when planning the maneuvers as a crew task, but the CRM content was concentrated in the first maneuvers and thinned out toward the end of the profile. The trend was toward assuming the division of duties rather than stating it. SP is expected to brief duties and knock-it-off criteria for every maneuver on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Application of the CRM concept when analyzing abnormal and emergency situations

texts.0: SP, due to absent explicit role assignment under load, did not apply the CRM concept when analyzing the simulated emergency and worked the problem alone while aircraft control degraded. SP stated no problem summary, allocated no tasks and used the other cockpit as no resource at all. The IP had to take control and direct the analysis.
texts.1: SP, due to absent explicit role assignment at the onset of the abnormal indication, kept both the flying and the analysis and let the aircraft state drift while reading the checklist. SP allocated duties only after the IP had stated the requirement more than once, and the analysis was completed late relative to the time available for the situation. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial attempt to handle the situation single-handed, began the analysis without allocating tasks between the cockpits. SP recognized the loading quickly, stated the problem in plain language, assigned the flying and the checklist duties explicitly and completed the analysis in time. No IP prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP applied the CRM concept to the maximum extent when analyzing the situation: the problem was stated in plain language, roles were allocated explicitly and the aircraft was flown throughout. The analysis was accurate and without delay and the response matched the published procedure.
texts.4: SP allocated roles within the first seconds of the abnormal indication, kept the aircraft flown and the analysis running in parallel, and reviewed the plan as the situation developed. The use of both cockpits as resources was complete and deviations from the expected standard were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard in analyzing the situation as a crew task, but the role allocation was made only after the first checklist step rather than at the onset of the indication. The trend was toward stating the division of duties once and not revisiting it as the situation developed. SP is expected to assign roles at recognition and to review them as the situation changes on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Communication and upward inquiry in the IP/SP cockpit

texts.0: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in stating 'unable' when the direction could not be complied with, continued a maneuver already assessed as outside his/her current capability and made no call to the other cockpit. The doubt stayed unspoken until the deviation was fully established. The IP had to intervene on the controls to recover the situation.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in the IP/SP cockpit, passed the doubt as an indirect hint instead of a direct statement of the aircraft state. SP stated the problem clearly only after the IP had questioned him/her twice, and the delay left the correction to the last usable point. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial reluctance to interrupt the IP, delayed the first call on the deviating parameter. SP recognized the delay, made a direct call using standard phraseology and corrected the deviation without assistance. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP communicated with the other cockpit accurately and without delay, used standard phraseology and stated 'unable' where the direction could not be complied with. Calls were made at the point where they were useful and all acknowledgements and readbacks were complete.
texts.4: SP kept the two cockpits on a common picture throughout the sortie with short, standard and timely calls, and questioned an assumption that the instruments did not support. Communication was unambiguous in both directions with negligible deviation from the expected standard.
texts.marginal: SP met the communication standard, but the calls to the other cockpit were reactive and made after the IP had opened the subject rather than at the moment of recognition. The trend was toward reporting the deviation only once it was visible to both crew members. SP is expected to make the first call at recognition and to state 'unable' without hesitation on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Debriefing self-assessment and identification of CRM development areas

texts.0: SP, due to reviewing the sortie only by maneuver outcome, took no part in the CRM discussion at the debriefing and offered no assessment of the coordination errors made in flight. SP attributed every deviation to external factors and identified no area for CRM development. The IP had to reconstruct the events and state the development areas without any input from SP, and the CRM box could be completed only on IP assessment.
texts.1: SP, due to reviewing the sortie only by maneuver outcome, described the events correctly but identified no CRM shortfall until the IP had raised each one verbally more than once. The development areas were finally accepted but SP did not connect them to the specific events of the sortie. No action beyond the extended debriefing was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially event-by-event rather than behavior-based review, missed the coordination element in the first deviation discussed. SP recognized this without prompting, restated the deviation in CRM terms and identified the development area unaided. No IP direction was required.
texts.3: SP took part fully in the CRM discussion, self-identified the coordination errors made in flight and stated specific areas for CRM development. The assessment was accurate, prompt and tied to identifiable events of the sortie.
texts.4: SP self-assessed the sortie in CRM terms before being asked, identified both the shortfalls and the points where CRM improved mission effectiveness and flight safety, and proposed specific corrective actions for the next sortie. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard in the debriefing, but the self-assessment stayed at the level of what happened rather than which CRM behavior was missing. The trend was toward naming a development area only for the deviation that was most obvious. SP is expected to review each item of the profile in CRM terms and to propose the corrective action himself/herself on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Transfer of A/C control with the exact words and positive assumption of control
error_modes.source: technique:1.15 Transfer of A/C and Systems Control

texts.0: SP, due to an unclear handover of aircraft control between IP and SP, released the controls after an informal call and did not wait for the other cockpit to positively assume control by shaking the control stick. For a short period neither pilot was flying the aircraft, and on the following exchange both pilots were on the controls at the same time. The IP had to take control, state 'I have the A/C' and stabilize the aircraft before the item could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to an unclear handover of aircraft control between the two cockpits, used 'it' and 'jet' in lieu of the term 'A/C' on most transfers and did not shake the control stick when assuming control. SP applied the exact phraseology only after the IP had corrected the wording twice, and one transfer had to be repeated because the intention was ambiguous. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a fast-paced exchange at the entry of the maneuver, made the first transfer without the required stick shake and with a non-standard word in place of 'A/C'. SP recognized the omission without prompting, repeated the transfer with the exact words and a noticeable stick shake, and every following exchange was standard. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP transferred aircraft control accurately and without delay, using 'you have the A/C' and 'I have the A/C' with a noticeable shake of the control stick on each exchange. SP never released the controls before the other pilot had positively assumed control, and relinquished control immediately when directed by the IP. All transfers during the sortie were unambiguous.
texts.4: SP used the exact transfer phraseology on every exchange, including the reversed order when the IP took control, and confirmed assumption of control with a clearly noticeable stick shake. SP queried the other cockpit immediately at the one point where the intention could have been read two ways. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the transfer of control standard, but the stick shake was weak enough that the IP had to look for it on two exchanges and the term 'A/C' was replaced once by 'it'. The trend across the sortie was toward shortening the phraseology as workload increased. SP is expected to use the full exact wording and a positive stick shake on every transfer on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Coordination of systems use under the last use, last in control logic
error_modes.source: technique:1.15 Transfer of A/C and Systems Control

texts.0: SP, due to an uncoordinated response between the two cockpits during the procedure, reconfigured the RMU and the GPS as pilot flying without any call to the other cockpit while the same pages were being worked there. The last use, last in control logic left the aircraft on a radio and navigation setup that neither pilot expected and the assigned frequency was lost. The IP had to take the systems, restore the configuration and direct the coordination before the profile could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to an uncoordinated response between the two cockpits, changed EFIS and canopy-related selections without stating the change and did not confirm which cockpit held the system. SP began announcing systems changes only after the IP had asked for the call twice, and two selections had to be reset. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to task focus during the configuration change, made the first RMU change without telling the other cockpit that he/she had taken the system. SP recognized the omission, stated the current setup and coordinated every following systems change including the handback to the pilot flying. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP coordinated systems use accurately and without delay, retaining the canopy, RMU, GPS and EFIS as pilot flying and clearly communicating each transfer of a system. SP stated when a system was passed to the other cockpit and when it was returned, so no inadvertent input occurred. The configuration was known to both cockpits throughout the sortie.
texts.4: SP coordinated every systems change before making it and confirmed the resulting configuration with the other cockpit, so the last use, last in control logic never produced an unexpected state. SP anticipated the points in the profile where both cockpits would work the same page and deconflicted them in advance. Deviations from the expected standard were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard for systems coordination, but the calls were made while the input was already being entered rather than before it, and one GPS change was announced only after the other cockpit questioned the display. The trend was toward assuming that the other pilot would notice the change. SP is expected to state and confirm who holds the system before each change on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Verbal compensation for the limited inter-cockpit visibility of the tandem seat

texts.0: SP, due to absent plain-language cross-talk on the changing aircraft state, assumed the configuration of the other cockpit instead of verifying it verbally and left the items controlled only from the opposite cockpit unaddressed for the whole sortie. SP flew with an altimeter setting that differed from the front cockpit and never asked for it, so the two cockpits worked from different altitude references. The IP had to stop the item, restore a common reference and direct the verbal checks before the profile could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to absent plain-language cross-talk between cockpits, did not confirm the systems that can only be manipulated or directly checked in the other cockpit and reported them as verified by assumption. SP asked for the altimeter setting and for the FCP-only selections only after the IP had prompted him/her more than once. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial reliance on what could be seen from his/her own cockpit, omitted the verbal confirmation of a system that cannot be checked from that seat. SP recognized the gap without prompting, asked the other cockpit for its state and cross-checked the altimeter setting before the next phase. No IP prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP compensated accurately and without delay for the lack of inter-cockpit visibility, asking for and reporting the state of every system that can only be checked or controlled from the opposite cockpit. Altimeter settings were cross-checked verbally between cockpits and intentions were stated rather than assumed. Both cockpits held the same picture of the aircraft configuration throughout.
texts.4: SP verbalized intentions and configuration before each phase, so the other cockpit never had to infer what was being done. SP confirmed the items that cannot be seen from the rear cockpit by the accepted indirect means and cross-checked both altimeter settings at every change. Deviations from the expected standard were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard for inter-cockpit verbal coordination, but the reports were answers to questions from the other cockpit rather than volunteered statements, and one altimeter change was cross-checked late. The trend was toward speaking only when asked. SP is expected to state configuration and intentions on his/her own initiative on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Checklist discipline and challenge and response on (BOTH) items

texts.0: SP, due to a lapse in which a briefed item was omitted under workload, gave lip service to a standardized mnemonic instead of actually performing the checklist item and treated a (BOTH) item as complete without any response from the other cockpit. SP then started the next checklist before the previous one had been confirmed complete, and the omission was carried into the following phase. The IP had to stop the sequence, run the checklist from the top and verify the omitted items before the profile could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to a lapse under increasing workload, did not positively confirm completion of two checklists and issued the (BOTH) challenges without waiting for the proper response. SP returned to the checklist only after the IP had directed it twice, and after the interruption resumed at the point of interruption instead of restarting two to three steps prior. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an interruption during the checklist, missed one step and initially continued from the point where the interruption had occurred. SP recognized the risk without prompting, restarted two to three steps prior to the missed step and completed the challenge and response with the other cockpit. No IP prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP maintained checklist discipline accurately and without delay, positively confirming completion of every checklist and completing each (BOTH) item by challenge and response with the other cockpit. Checklists were run without interruption and no new checklist was started before the previous one was complete. Verbal challenges such as 'on, normal, normal, good blinker' were made with the exact wording.
texts.4: SP executed a few items from memory and then referenced the checklist page to verify completion, so no item was left unconfirmed at any point of the sortie. SP obtained a proper response for every (BOTH) item and did not refer to the checklist during critical phases of flight, catching the items up immediately afterwards. Deviations from the expected standard were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the checklist discipline standard, but the (BOTH) challenges were made as statements and the response from the other cockpit was accepted as given on two items. The trend was toward relying on the mnemonic rather than on the checklist page for verification. SP is expected to obtain and acknowledge a proper response on every (BOTH) item on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Task management: setting priorities and altering the course of action on new information

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the busy phase of the sortie, held the original plan after information had arrived that invalidated it and worked secondary cockpit tasks before the flying task. Priorities were never re-established and the required actions of that phase were left undone until the profile could no longer be flown as briefed. The IP had to take the aircraft, reset the priorities and re-sequence the tasks before the item could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to inadequate workload management, kept every task in the sequence in which it had been planned and shed nothing when workload increased. SP altered the course of action only after the IP had pointed out the new information twice, and the change was then made one phase later than it was useful. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the cockpit workload inside the turn, initially continued with a secondary task instead of the flying task. SP recognized the misordering without prompting, shed the secondary task and re-established the correct priorities before the parameters diverged. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP managed the cockpit tasks accurately and without delay, establishing priorities for each phase and altering the course of action when new information required it. Available resources and automation were used to reduce workload and standard operating procedures were complied with throughout. All required actions were completed within the phase to which they belonged.
texts.4: SP sequenced the cockpit tasks so that each high-workload segment was entered with the secondary work already complete. SP revised the plan at the first item of information that changed it and stated the revised priorities to the other cockpit. Deviations from the expected standard were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the task management standard, but priorities were re-established only once the workload was already high, and one secondary task was carried into a phase where it should have been shed. The trend was toward working the planned sequence rather than the current situation. SP is expected to re-prioritize at the moment new information is received on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Operational Risk Management: assessment of environmental, mission and pilot factors

texts.0: SP, due to an ORM assessment completed as a checkbox without any mitigation of the identified threats, did not assess environmental conditions, mission profile or pilot factors before the sortie. SP proposed no mission change for risks that were already known at briefing time and treated risk as something to be completely eliminated rather than matched to the mission. The IP had to conduct the risk assessment and impose the mission changes before the profile could be flown.
texts.1: SP, due to a caution-range ORM score that was treated as if it were green, identified the risk factors but attached no mitigation to any of them. SP proposed acceptable mission changes only after the IP had raised each factor separately, and the changes came after planning was otherwise complete. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed risk assessment during mission planning, initially left the pilot factors out of the assessment. SP recognized the omission without prompting, completed the assessment and proposed a mission change that reduced the risk without degrading the training value. No IP prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP applied ORM accurately and without delay, assessing environmental conditions, mission profile and pilot factors and reducing the identified risks to an acceptable level. The mitigations proposed did not negatively impact the training objectives and the trade of training benefit against risk was stated explicitly. All risk factors relevant to the sortie were covered.
texts.4: SP assessed the risk factors before the briefing and arrived with a mitigation already matched to each of them. SP re-assessed the risk in flight when one factor changed and adjusted the profile without loss of training value. Deviations from the expected standard were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the ORM standard, but the assessment covered the environmental conditions in detail and the pilot factors only in general terms. The trend was toward completing the assessment for the record rather than using it to shape the mission. SP is expected to attach a specific mitigation to every identified risk on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Situational awareness in flight and emergency recovery plan established before the emergency

texts.0: SP, due to absent contingency management in the pre-takeoff brief, entered the working area with no emergency recovery plan established and allowed a minor system indication to cause distraction during a critical phase of flight. Clearing turns were not flown and the aircraft systems went unmonitored while SP worked the distraction. The IP had to take the aircraft, clear the airspace and establish the recovery plan before the item could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to a recovery plan that was never established before it was needed, could not name the recovery field or the route to it when asked in flight. SP cleared the airspace and resumed monitoring the aircraft systems only after the IP had directed it more than once, and the distraction was carried through most of the maneuver entry. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to attention drawn to a secondary indication, interrupted the lookout and the systems scan for the first part of the maneuver. SP recognized the lapse without prompting, cleared the airspace, restored the scan and restated the emergency recovery plan for the area in use. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP maintained situational awareness accurately and without delay, clearing the airspace before each maneuver and monitoring the aircraft systems throughout. The emergency recovery plan was established before it was needed and updated as the aircraft moved between areas. Distractions were absorbed without loss of aircraft control or of the briefed parameters.
texts.4: SP kept a continuous perception of the aircraft in relation to the airspace, the weather and the fuel state and forecast the tasks each phase would require. The emergency recovery plan was stated for every area entered and revised as the conditions changed. Deviations from the expected standard were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard for situational awareness, but the emergency recovery plan was formed once at the briefing and never updated as the sortie moved away from the field. The trend was toward clearing the airspace at area entry only and not between successive maneuvers. SP is expected to update the recovery plan and clear the airspace before each maneuver on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Crew coordination during emergency ground egress and return to apron
error_modes.source: technique:3.15 ABNORMAL PROCEDURES (incl. 3.15.1 Emergency Ground Egress, 3.15.2 Return to Apron)

texts.0: SP, due to a CRM breakdown in which the required behavior of explicit role assignment was not performed, worked the egress sequence out of order and turned the battery and generator off before the actions that require intercom with the other cockpit. Coordination was lost, the ISS was not confirmed in SOLO and the seat pins were not installed. The IP had to stop the drill, restore the sequence and direct the actions before it could be completed.
texts.1: SP, due to inadequate crew coordination between front and rear cockpit, performed the egress actions without announcing them and did not notify the controlling agency that assistance was required. SP completed the sequence in the correct order only after the IP had prompted him/her twice, and the parking brake and the hands clear signal were left to the end. No IP intervention beyond the verbal direction was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a fast start to the drill, began the shutdown before confirming that the aircraft was at a complete stop with the parking brake set. SP recognized the mis-ordering without prompting, restated the sequence to the other cockpit and completed the remaining actions in order, with the battery and generator turned off just before egress. No IP direction was needed.
texts.3: SP performed the emergency ground egress in a systematic and deliberate manner, coordinating each action with the other cockpit as it was made. The aircraft was brought to a complete stop with the parking brake set, the engine was shut down, the ISS was confirmed in SOLO and both cockpit seat pins were installed. The battery and generator were turned off just before egress so intercom remained available, and the controlling agency was notified in time.
texts.4: SP led the egress with clear role assignment and confirmation from the other cockpit at each step and actuated no switch without informing the ground crew. The hands clear signal was given with the parking brake set once inspection was required, and the After Landing Checklist items were properly executed when returning to apron. Deviations from the expected standard were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard for the ground egress drill, but the coordination calls were made after each action rather than before it and the notification to the controlling agency was late. The trend was toward performing the memorized sequence alone rather than as a crew. SP is expected to announce and confirm each egress step with the other cockpit on the next sortie.
